passage: I'm Asif. Before the maths test, Karthik sat next to me wringing his hands, one over the other, again and again. I thought he must be nervous. I almost said nothing because I didn't want to make it worse. Then I whispered, “You okay?” He said, “I always forget the formulas.” I said, “Me too. Want to go through the area one quickly?” We did it for two minutes, and his hands stopped. I don't know if that was the only reason, because it was cold in the room too. But it helped a bit.

qa.q: What was Karthik doing with his hands before the test?
qa.a: He was wringing his hands, one over the other, again and again.

qa.q: What did Asif think Karthik was feeling, and how sure can he be?
qa.a: He thought Karthik was nervous, and Karthik said he always forgets the formulas, which fits. Asif admits he cannot be sure, since the room was also cold.

qa.q: What small step helped Karthik?
qa.a: Asif asked quietly if he was okay and offered to go through the formula together, which gave Karthik something concrete to do.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel when Asif whispered to him?
qa.a: Probably relieved that somebody noticed and did not make a fuss, and less alone with his worry.

grounding: A child sees a classmate wring the hands before a test, reads nervousness, and offers a friendly word.

passage: Note from Hafsa, Class 5 teacher. Before the spelling test I saw Noor wringing her hands under the desk. I could not tell if she was nervous or just cold from the fan. I bent down and asked quietly how she felt about the test. She said, “I keep thinking I'll go blank.” I told her she could take a slow breath and begin with the words she knows best. Her hands loosened. I did not tell the class. I will check in with her privately before the next test and ask what helped.

qa.q: Where did Hafsa see Noor wringing her hands?
qa.a: She saw Noor wringing her hands under the desk.

qa.q: What was Noor most likely feeling, and what else could explain her hands?
qa.a: Most likely she was nervous about going blank in the test, as she told Hafsa. Cold from the fan could also have made her wring her hands.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do that helped, and what will she do next?
qa.a: She asked quietly and privately and offered a way to start, and she will check in before the next test to ask what helped.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel when Noor's hands loosen?
qa.a: Hafsa is probably relieved that the quiet advice helped, and plans to check in with Noor privately before the next test.

grounding: Wringing hands before a test suggests nervousness though it does not prove it; a friendly word helps.

passage: Thursday. Harish's diary. Before the Hindi test, Vishal sat at his desk twisting his hands round and round, like he was wringing out a wet towel. I thought, He's scared of the test, like me. So I leaned over and said, “Want to go over the matras? I keep mixing them up too.” He shook his head. Then he said, really quietly, “My Dadi went to hospital last night.” I didn't know what to say, so I just sat closer till the bell. I told Ma'am at break, and she let Vishal phone home at lunch. So it wasn't the test at all.

qa.q: Where did Vishal's Dadi go last night?
qa.a: Vishal's Dadi went to hospital last night.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling as he wrung his hands?
qa.a: He was worried and frightened about his Dadi in hospital; Harish first guessed test nerves, which shows the hands alone didn't reveal the cause.

qa.q: Which of Harish's choices helped most, and why?
qa.a: Offering a friendly word opened the door, and telling Ma'am meant Vishal got to phone home at lunch.

qa.q: How did Harish first read the wringing hands?
qa.a: Harish assumed it was test nerves, because that's what Harish felt too, before hearing the real reason.

grounding: Shows a child reading a classmate's hand-wringing as test nerves, offering a friendly word, and finding a different cause.

passage: The oral test was the first thing that winter morning at the village school, and the inspector's jeep was already outside. Yusuf sat on the bench wringing his hands, squeezing and twisting his fingers over and over. Zubin watched. He's terrified. Zubin slid along the bench. “You know the tables better than anyone. You taught me seven.” Yusuf blew on his fingers and gave a small smile. “Thanks. I am scared. But I also did the milking at five, and my hands are frozen stiff.” Zubin laughed and rubbed his own cold hands. “Then let's warm them up together.”

qa.q: When did Yusuf do the milking?
qa.a: Yusuf did the milking at five.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling as he wrung his hands?
qa.a: Yusuf was scared of the oral test, as he admitted, but his hands were also frozen stiff from the early milking.

qa.q: Why was Zubin's friendly word a good choice?
qa.a: It reminded Yusuf of his real skill and showed support, whatever the cause of the hand-wringing.

qa.q: How did Zubin first read Yusuf's hands?
qa.a: Zubin thought Yusuf was terrified, which was partly right, but the cold was another reason he hadn't guessed.

grounding: Shows a child reading a classmate's hand-wringing as nerves, offering a kind word, and finding cold was part of it too.

passage: Before the spelling test in their Dublin classroom, Clara noticed Liam at the next desk rubbing and twisting his hands together, round and round, head down. Poor Liam, she thought. He always panics. She tore a corner off her page, wrote You'll be grand! with a smiley face, and slid it over. Liam read it, then held up his hands. They were shiny. “Sanitiser,” he whispered. “Too much. It won't dry.” Clara snorted. Then he added, “But thanks. I am a bit nervous about ‘necessary’.” She wrote on the corner: one collar, two sleeves. He grinned.

qa.q: What was on Liam's hands?
qa.a: Liam had too much sanitiser on his hands.

qa.q: What was Liam feeling before the test?
qa.a: Liam was a bit nervous about spelling “necessary”, though the hand-twisting was mostly from sanitiser that wouldn't dry.

qa.q: What made Clara's note a good choice even though she guessed wrong?
qa.a: A friendly word helps whatever the cause, and it led Liam to share his real worry, so Clara could help with the spelling 🙂

qa.q: How did Clara read Liam's twisting hands?
qa.a: Clara thought he was panicking as usual, not realising sanitiser explained most of it.

grounding: Shows a child reading a classmate's hand-twisting as worry, a friendly word helping, and the signal alone not proving the cause.

passage:
Outside the exam hall, Shankar noticed Gurpreet on the bench, twisting her hands round and round as if wringing out a wet cloth. Scared of the maths paper, he guessed. He sat beside her. "You know fractions better than me. You'll be fine."

Gurpreet gave a small smile. "It's not the paper. My little brother had a fever all night, and Mummy took him to the clinic this morning. I keep thinking about him."

Shankar was quiet for a moment. Then he offered her a piece of his jaggery. "Maybe ask the office if you can phone home at lunch?"

Her hands went still.

qa.q: Where did Mummy take Gurpreet's little brother that morning?
qa.a: To the clinic.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet worried about as she wrung her hands?
qa.a: She was anxious about her little brother, who had a fever all night, not mainly about the maths paper as Shankar had guessed.

qa.q: What did Shankar do that helped, even though his guess was wrong?
qa.a: He sat beside her with a friendly word, which gave her a chance to share the real worry, and then suggested phoning home at lunch.

qa.q: How did Shankar read the hand-wringing at first?
qa.a: Shankar took it as fear of the maths paper, and learned that the same signal can come from a different worry.

grounding: It shows a child reading a classmate's hand-wringing before a test as nervousness, offering a friendly word, and learning the cause was different.
